English avatar Borrowed from Hindustani अवतार (avtār) / اوتار (avtār), from Sanskrit अवतार (avatāra, “descent of a deity from a heaven”), a compound of अव (ava, “off, away, down”) and the vṛddhi-stem of the root तॄ (tṝ, “to cross”) (whence तरति (tarati)). From French avalanche, from Franco-Provençal (Savoy) avalançhe, blend of aval (“downhill”) and standard lavençhe, from Vulgar Latin *labanka (compare Occitan lavanca, Italian valanga), of uncertain origin, perhaps an alteration of Late Latin lābīna (“landslide”) (compare Franco-Provençal (Dauphiné) lavino, Romansh lavina), from Latin lābēs, from lābor (“to slip, slide”).

senses.d: A large mass or body of snow and ice sliding swiftly down a mountain side, or falling down a precipice.
ex: They were drinking from a fountain / That was pouring like an avalanche / Coming down the mountain

senses.d: A fall of earth, rocks, etc., similar to that of an avalanche of snow or ice.
A sudden, great, or irresistible descent or influx; anything like an avalanche in suddenness and overwhelming quantity.
ex: I stepped into an avalanche, it covered up my soul

senses.d: To descend like an avalanche.
ex:
Soon the sun’s warmth makes them shed crystal shells

As it happened, I had progressed only some few feet out onto the snow when a clean-cut section stripped off the surface and avalanched.

senses.d: To come down upon; to overwhelm.
ex: The shelf broke and the boxes avalanched the workers.
The applications were doubtless snowed under in the maze of official correspondence which avalanched the new government.

senses.d: To propel downward like an avalanche.
ex: Then another misfortune avalanched itself upon me, before even I had fully taken in the extent of the first.
